expectedText:
LABOR RIGHTS REGARDLESS OF IMMIGRATION STATUS (LABOR CODE § 1171.5) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Corp.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes Labor Code § 1171.5, which declares that the protections, rights, and remedies available under California labor and employment law extend to workers regardless of immigration status, subject to a federal-law limit on reinstatement, and which restricts inquiry into a person's immigration status in a proceeding to enforce those laws. It does not cover the corpus's separate Immigrant Worker Protection Act document, which addresses a different subject — restrictions on an employer's cooperation with federal immigration enforcement at the worksite, such as agent access to nonpublic areas and notice around an I-9 inspection — rather than the scope of the underlying labor-law protections addressed here.

PROTECTIONS, RIGHTS, AND REMEDIES AVAILABLE REGARDLESS OF IMMIGRATION STATUS
Labor Code § 1171.5(a) declares that all protections, rights, and remedies available under California state law — with one exception for a reinstatement remedy that federal law prohibits — are available to every individual regardless of immigration status who has applied for employment, or who is or has been employed, in California.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "(a) All protections, rights, and remedies available under state law, except any reinstatement remedy prohibited by federal law, are available to all individuals regardless of immigration status who have applied for employment, or who are or who have been employed, in this state."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1171.5(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 1171.5(a), as amended by Stats. 2017, Ch. 160, Sec. 4 (AB 1690), eff. Jan. 1, 2018 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1171.5.)
  Known gap: This subdivision states that 'all protections, rights, and remedies' are available regardless of immigration status 'except any reinstatement remedy prohibited by federal law,' but the statute itself does not say which reinstatement remedies federal law actually prohibits; that is left to case law construing the federal Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, addressed in a separate clause of this document citing Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co. This document does not resolve, for any specific employment situation, whether a federal-law reinstatement bar would apply.

IMMIGRATION STATUS IS IRRELEVANT TO LIABILITY; RESTRICTION ON INQUIRY
Labor Code § 1171.5(b) states that, for purposes of enforcing state labor, employment, civil rights, consumer protection, and housing laws, a person's immigration status is irrelevant to the issue of liability. It further provides that, in a proceeding or discovery undertaken to enforce those state laws, no inquiry into a person's immigration status is permitted unless the party seeking to make the inquiry has shown, by clear and convincing evidence, that the inquiry is necessary to comply with federal immigration law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "(b) For purposes of enforcing state labor, employment, civil rights, consumer protection, and housing
						laws, a person’s immigration status is irrelevant to the issue of liability, and in proceedings or discovery undertaken to enforce those state laws no inquiry shall be permitted into a person’s immigration status unless the person seeking to make this inquiry has shown by clear and convincing evidence that the inquiry is necessary in order to comply with federal immigration law."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1171.5(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 1171.5(b), as amended by Stats. 2017, Ch. 160, Sec. 4 (AB 1690), eff. Jan. 1, 2018 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1171.5.)
  Known gap: The raw HTML for this subdivision contains two formatting artifacts that both independently fetched copies (using two distinct User-Agent strings on 2026-09-07) reproduced identically: a non-breaking space, rather than an ordinary space, immediately after '(b)', and a mid-sentence line wrap — a newline followed by six tab characters — between 'housing' and 'laws'. Both are preserved exactly in the quote below rather than silently normalized. The statute does not itself define what showing would satisfy the 'clear and convincing evidence' standard for when an immigration-status inquiry is 'necessary...to comply with federal immigration law,' and this document does not resolve that open question for any specific proceeding.

DECLARATORY OF EXISTING LAW; SEVERABILITY
Labor Code § 1171.5(c) states that the section is declaratory of existing law. Subdivision (d) makes the section's provisions severable: if any provision, or its application, is held invalid, that invalidity does not affect other provisions or applications that can still be given effect.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "(c) The provisions of this section are declaratory of existing law.(d) The provisions of this section are severable. If any provision of this section or its application is held invalid, that invalidity shall not affect other provisions or applications that can be given effect without the invalid provision or application."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1171.5(c)-(d) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), Cal. Lab. Code § 1171.5(c)-(d), as amended by Stats. 2017, Ch. 160, Sec. 4 (AB 1690), eff. Jan. 1, 2018 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1171.5.)
  Known gap: The raw HTML renders subdivisions (c) and (d) as adjacent paragraph elements with no visible space between the period ending (c) and the '(d)' marker that follows it — both independently fetched copies reproduced this identically, and the quote below preserves it exactly rather than inserting a space that is not in the source. Subdivision (c)'s statement that the section is 'declaratory of existing law' is a legislative characterization; this document does not independently verify what specific pre-2002 case law or statute the Legislature understood itself to be declaratory of, beyond what is addressed in a separate clause of this document citing Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co.

WHY THE STATUTE WAS ENACTED: THE 2002 RESPONSE TO HOFFMAN PLASTIC COMPOUNDS
Section 1171.5 originated in Senate Bill No. 1818 (2002), a package of four nearly identical provisions added across the Civil, Government, Health and Safety, and Labor Codes. The California Supreme Court has explained that the Legislature enacted SB 1818 the same year the U.S. Supreme Court decided Hoffman Plastic Compounds, Inc. v. NLRB (2002) 535 U.S. 137 — a case holding that the National Labor Relations Board could not award backpay to an undocumented worker for a violation of federal labor law — in order to ensure that unauthorized workers in California would continue to receive the same protections and remedies as other workers under the state's own employment and labor laws, apart from reinstatement when federal law prohibits it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "to ensure that in California unauthorized alien workers would continue to have the same protections and remedies (apart from reinstatement when prohibited by federal law) afforded other workers under California’s employment and labor laws."
  — Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co., 59 Cal. 4th 407, 420 (2014) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2680642/salas-v-sierra-chemical-co/)
  Known gap: This clause describes Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co.'s account of why SB 1818 was enacted, not an independent legislative-history source such as a committee report; this document did not separately verify that legislative history beyond what the Salas opinion itself states. The Salas preemption analysis discussed elsewhere in this document was decided in a case about FEHA discrimination and retaliation claims specifically; the opinion does not purport to resolve preemption for every other California labor and employment statute that § 1171.5(a) says is available regardless of immigration status. This document also does not independently verify Hoffman Plastic Compounds' own holding against the U.S. Reports text; it relies on the Salas court's characterization of that holding.

SECTION 1171.5 IS ONE OF FOUR NEARLY IDENTICAL STATUTES
Labor Code § 1171.5 was enacted alongside three companion provisions using substantially the same operative language: Civil Code § 3339, Government Code § 7285, and Health and Safety Code § 24000. The California Supreme Court has noted a wording difference among them in how each historically defined the category of state law covered by its subdivision (b).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "The language of Civil Code section 3339 and Government Code section 7285 is the same. The language of the other two provisions- — Health and Safety Code section 24000 and Labor Code section 1171.5 — differs only in the wording of subdivision (b). While Civil Code section 3339 and Government Code section 7285 refer to “state labor, employment, civil rights, and employee housing laws,” Health and Safety Code section 24000 and Labor Code section 1171.5 both refer only to “state labor and employment laws.”"
  — Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co., 59 Cal. 4th 407, 419 n.2 (2014) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2680642/salas-v-sierra-chemical-co/)
  Known gap: This footnote reflects Labor Code § 1171.5(b)'s wording as it existed when Salas was decided in 2014 — the footnote states that subdivision (b) then referred only to 'state labor and employment laws.' Labor Code § 1171.5 was subsequently amended by Stats. 2017, Ch. 160, § 4 (AB 1690), effective January 1, 2018, and the current text of subdivision (b) — quoted in a separate clause of this document from a 2026 fetch of leginfo.legislature.ca.gov — now refers to 'state labor, employment, civil rights, consumer protection, and housing laws,' bringing its wording closer to Government Code § 7285's wording as Salas described it, though this document does not verify whether the two are now identical. This document does not independently fetch or verify the current text of Civil Code § 3339, Government Code § 7285, or Health and Safety Code § 24000 themselves.

A FEDERAL-LAW LIMIT COURTS HAVE APPLIED TO THIS SECTION'S REMEDIES
Section 1171.5(a) makes 'all protections, rights, and remedies' available regardless of immigration status, 'except any reinstatement remedy prohibited by federal law.' Applying that framework to a FEHA discrimination and retaliation claim, the California Supreme Court held that federal immigration law does not preempt an award of lost pay for the period before an employer discovers a worker's ineligibility to work in the United States under federal law, but does preempt such an award for the period after that discovery — because continuing to employ a worker known to be unauthorized is itself prohibited by federal immigration law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-07]
  "to the extent that it makes a California FEHA lost pay award available to an unauthorized alien worker for the postdiscovery period."
  — Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co., 59 Cal. 4th 407, 424 (2014) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2680642/salas-v-sierra-chemical-co/)
  Known gap: This holding was reached in a case applying California's FEHA specifically. In the raw opinion text, this sentence is immediately followed by a footnote marker and a full footnote (numbered 3 in the opinion) before the sentence's continuation resumes on the next page; this quote reproduces only the continuation clause that appears after that footnote, not the words immediately preceding the footnote marker on the prior page, so as to avoid quoting across that intervening footnote as if it were contiguous text. That footnote itself states that the court's preemption analysis for the post-discovery period is limited to an employer who discovers a worker's unauthorized status after the worker has already been discharged or not rehired — the court left open, as a distinct situation, an employer who knowingly hired or continued to employ an unauthorized worker in the first place; this document does not quote that footnote. The quoted continuation clause also contains a mid-sentence line wrap in the raw opinion text (a literal newline between "an" and "unauthorized," verified directly against the source), normalized to a single space here rather than reproduced as a literal newline. This document does not address whether or how this same prediscovery/post-discovery distinction has been applied by any court to a California labor statute other than FEHA, and does not resolve whether a specific reinstatement or lost-pay remedy in a specific case would or would not be found preempted.

RELATIONSHIP TO OTHER DOCUMENTS IN THIS CORPUS
This document addresses only Labor Code § 1171.5's extension of state labor and employment law protections, rights, and remedies to workers regardless of immigration status. It does not cover the corpus's separate Immigrant Worker Protection Act document, which instead restricts an employer's cooperation with federal immigration enforcement at the worksite — including access by immigration enforcement agents to nonpublic areas and to employee records, and notice to employees around a federal immigration inspection of I-9 forms. It also does not cover the definition of a 'protected individual' used elsewhere in this corpus for national-origin or citizenship-status discrimination claims, which draws on a different body of law — federal immigration-related unfair employment practices — from the state-law remedies-and-liability statute addressed here.

WHAT THIS DOCUMENT DOES AND DOES NOT DO
This document states the text of Labor Code § 1171.5 and describes how one California appellate court has applied it in a reported decision. It does not determine, for any specific employment relationship, what protections, rights, or remedies are or are not available, whether a particular inquiry into a specific person's immigration status would or would not meet the 'clear and convincing evidence' standard the statute describes, or whether a federal-law reinstatement bar would or would not apply in a specific case.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge that you have received and read this document.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Company: Acme Corp.
Date: September 7, 2026
City, State: Sacramento, California
